RackTrack · where we are

Photo, Network, Record

A photo of a rack should become a correct record, checked against the live network. This is what we built, what works, and what is missing.

18 September 2026demo.racktrack.aiNetBox 4.6ServiceNow dev322173Tracked as SPRTMS-1636

01 · The three layers

One rack exists in three places at once

The whole job is to make those three agree. Each one knows something the other two do not, and each one can be wrong in its own way. The picture below is the map of the work: two of the three connections are working today, one is not built yet.

Read it as three boxes and three lines. Each line is a question: does this side agree with that one.

Physical

The photo

A person stands at the rack and takes one picture. The app finds each box in it and works out which shelf it sits on.

  • KnowsHow many boxes, where each one sits, how it looks, the labels stuck on it
  • Cannot knowThe name the network calls it, its serial number, which cable goes where
  • Gets it wrongWhen two boxes look the same, or a label is hidden or dirty
Logical

The network

Each managed switch is asked about itself over the network, by SNMP. It answers with its own facts and with what it can see on its cables.

  • KnowsIts name, make, model, serial, every port, what is plugged in, its neighbours
  • Cannot knowWhich shelf it sits on, what the rack looks like, anything about a box with no network brain
  • Gets it wrongRarely. This is the most trustworthy of the three
Database

The record

NetBox is what the company believes it owns. It is what people plan from, bill from and audit against, so it must never be written carelessly.

  • KnowsEvery rack, device, port and cable the company has written down, and who looks after each one
  • Cannot knowAnything that was never typed in, and anything that changed since
  • Gets it wrongWhenever the real world moved and nobody updated it. This is the whole reason RackTrack exists
The lineThe question it answersWhere it standsWhat it needs
Photo to recordIs the rack really as the record says it isWorkingBuilt, live, proved end to end
Network to recordDo the switch facts reach the recordWorkingBuilt, live
Photo to networkWhich box in the photo is which switch on the networkNot built yetDesign reworked this week, build next

Why the missing line matters. Today the app can put a rack into the record, and it can read the switches. What it cannot yet say with confidence is that the box on the third shelf from the top is the switch the network calls SW02. Until it can, the rich detail from the network cannot be attached to the right box with certainty, and a person has to say which is which by hand.

02 · Photo to record

From a picture of a rack to a change in the record

This line works today and is live on the demo. It is the careful one: the record belongs to the customer, so nothing is written until a named person has been to the rack and an admin has approved it. Every screen below is the real system.

1

Take one photo of the rack

Technician

The person at the rack opens the app and photographs the front of it. That is the whole job at the rack. They do not type an inventory and they never edit the record.

The app draws a box around each device it finds and works out which shelf each one is on. In this rack it found five: a router at shelf 16, a switch at 14, a patch panel across 11 and 12, a switch at 9, and a patch panel across 6 and 7.

Why shelves matter: a shelf number is the one handle the photo and the record share, so it is how a box in the picture is tied to a row in the database.
2

Compare the photo with the record

App

The app reads the record for that rack and lines the two up, shelf by shelf. It never changes anything here. It only produces a list of differences.

On this rack the answer was nine things do not match, all of them devices the record has never heard of, plus twelve supporting rows that would be created with them.

Each difference is one of three things: something here that is not in the record, something in the record that is not here, or the same thing with different details. Nothing is ever deleted.
3

Show who it is going to, before sending

AppAdded this week

Before the technician sends anything, the app names the person who will pick it up. It reads the rack's own single point of contact out of the record.

If the app can match the photo to a rack the customer has set up in that room, it names that rack's contact. If the record names nobody, it says plainly that the admin will choose.

BeforeThe technician sent it and hoped. They learned who had it only after the fact.
AfterThe name, the job title and the email are on the screen before the send.
4

Send it, and change nothing

Technician

The send puts the list in the admin's inbox. At this moment nothing has been written to the record, and the technician has no button that could write anything. The server refuses it, not just the screen.

This is the rule the whole design rests on: the person at the rack reports what they saw, they do not decide.

5

The admin sees the list and hands each item to somebody

Admin

The admin opens the check on the website. Every difference is listed in plain words. The admin cannot approve anything yet: first it has to go to a person who can walk to the rack and look.

The rack's own contact is offered first, because the record names them. The admin can pick somebody else, and often will.

6

Assign, and the ticket goes to the person actually chosen

AdminFixed this week

Choosing a person raises a real incident in ServiceNow and sends them an email. This used to be addressed to the rack's listed contact even when the admin had picked somebody else. Now it goes to whoever was chosen.

7

A real ticket, in the customer's own system

ServiceNow

The incident carries the rack, the difference and a link back. It lives in the customer's normal queue, so this work is tracked the way all their other work is tracked.

8

The person goes to the rack and answers

Assignee

They look, then resolve the ticket with what they found. Their answer is written back against the item.

A resolved ticket is not an approval. It is evidence. The item goes back to the admin with the finding attached, and the admin still has to decide.
9

The admin approves, and only then is the record written

AdminLive

Approve or reject, item by item, with the finding in front of them. Only approved items are written. Before writing, the app checks the record has not changed since the list was made; if it has, it stops and asks for a fresh comparison rather than writing over somebody else's work.

Nothing is ever deleted. A thing that is in the record but not in the rack is reported, never removed.

The promise this line makes. Save it once and the records appear. Save the same rack again and nothing changes at all. Nothing is deleted, ever. An automatic test runs the whole journey on every change and proves those three things still hold.

03 · Network to record

From a live switch to the record

This line works too. A managed switch can be asked about itself, and it answers with facts no camera can see. The question this page does not yet answer is which box in the photo that switch is, which is the missing link in section 04.

1

Add each managed switch

Admin or technician

A switch is added by its address. Two ways to read it, and the app picks whichever can reach it:

  • From the server, when the server sits on the same network as the switches.
  • From the phone itself, when the person is on site and the server is not on that network. A browser cannot open the kind of connection SNMP needs, so the phone app does it natively.

This rack has none added yet, which is why the screen says so. That is the honest state of this demo rack, not an error.

2

The switch answers with its own facts

Switch

Make, model, serial number, firmware, every port and whether it is in use, the VLANs, and the neighbours it can see on its cables. Every value on this screen came from the switch itself, not from a person and not from a guess.

The screen shown here is filling in from a different source at the same time: the make and model being read off the label in the rack photo. Those two sources meeting is exactly what section 04 is about.
3

Ports, cables and neighbours join the picture of the rack

App

The report puts the two together: the rack as the camera saw it, with port counts, port state and neighbours from the switches laid over it. On this rack, 79 of 164 ports are in use.

Where two switches can see each other on a cable, the app draws that cable. It only draws one when both ends agree, or it marks it as heard from one end only.

4

Those facts ride into the record with the approval

Admin

When the admin approves, the switch facts go into the record along with the boxes: the real model instead of a guess from the photo, the serial number, the ports, and the cables between switches. The approval path is exactly the one in section 02. There is no separate back door for network data.

04 · Photo to network

The missing link: which box is which switch

This is the one line of the picture that is not built. It sounds small and it is not. Without it, everything the network knows has to be attached to a box in the photo by a person, or by a guess.

1

Where it would happen

Empty today

The app already has a screen for it, called Review. It is where a person says "this switch is that box". It is empty on this rack because no switches have been read yet.

The screen exists. What is missing is the thinking behind it: a way to say which box is which with evidence, and to refuse when the evidence is not good enough.

2

What it does today, and why that is not good enough

Today the app proposes a match from two things only: how many ports the box appears to have, and who made it. That is all the photo and the switch share.

SituationWhat happens todayIs that safe
One 48 port switch, one 8 port switchMatched correctly by port countFine
Two switches of the same size in one rackWhichever came first in the list wins. Reverse the list and the answer swapsNot safe
A proposal nobody looked atThe app saves its own proposal, and later screens show it as factNot safe
A switch that is a stack of three boxesIt answers as one, so it can only ever be tied to one boxKnown gap

Our own office is the proof. We have two identical switches in one rack. Nothing in the photo or in the port count can tell them apart. Any design that cannot say "I do not know" on those two is a design that will quietly write the wrong answer into a customer's record.

3

The design we will build, after the first one was rejected

Reworked

The first design went to three independent reviewers whose only job was to break it. All three did. Here is what came out of that, in plain terms:

  • A device is every hardware fact we have seen for it, not one. Its serial number and its hardware addresses together. The same switch gave the phone a serial and gave the server an address, so keying on one fact alone would have split one switch into two devices.
  • Only a person's choice, box by box, counts as confirmed. Pressing one Apply button for the whole rack never does. Two identical switches show a blank, not a guess.
  • The box is always saved as it is today. Confidence controls only the extra detail that comes from the network: model, serial, ports, cables. That way the line that already works can never be broken by this new one.
  • The first version writes confirmed matches only. Probable and possible are shown to a person, never written.
  • Evidence is ranked and recorded. A serial read from the hardware outranks a name typed by a person, which outranks a port count. Whatever was used is kept with the match, so anybody can see why.
  • A teammate's rack planner is reused here. Its drawing of a rack shelf by shelf will show each match on a picture of the rack, and its table of how many shelves each kind of device takes will rule out any match whose size cannot fit.
  • Honest testing. Our two identical switches are the perfect test for "refuse to guess". Anything that needs hardware we do not own is built and clearly marked as untested.
4

What it will look like when it is done

The Review screen shows each switch beside the rack drawing, with the shelf it is proposed for and the evidence behind the proposal in one line: the serial matched, or the name matched, or only the port count matched. A person confirms one box at a time. Two identical switches sit there unconfirmed until somebody looks at a label, and the app says so instead of choosing.

Once confirmed, the network facts flow into the record attached to the right box, through the same approval path as everything else.

05 · What we built

What we built, in the order we built it

Eight pieces. The first four are live on the demo. The next three are built and tested and waiting for one deployment. The last one is a large change under way now.

  1. A safe way to change the record

    Live

    The whole compare, assign, ticket, resolve, approve, write path in section 02. This is the foundation everything else sits on.

  2. The ticket reaches the right person

    Live

    The ticket and the email used to go to the rack's listed contact even when the admin had picked somebody else. Now they go to whoever was actually chosen. At the same time, each organisation was walled off so it can only ever see its own work.

  3. The app recognises the rack

    Live

    A photo used to get a made up code that the record had never heard of, so the app fell back to a general site contact. Now, when a rack has been set up in a room, the app matches the photo to that rack and finds the rack's own contact. When it cannot be sure, it does not guess: it says the admin will choose.

    Proved on the live system: the same rack that used to name the site's general contact now names the rack's own contact, on the phone, before sending.

  4. A safety test for the whole path

    Live

    One automatic test drives the full journey and proves three promises: the first save creates the records, a second save of the same rack changes nothing, and nothing is ever deleted. Every later change has to keep all three true or the test fails.

  5. No more duplicate racks

    Live since 18 September

    Two photos of one rack used to become two racks in the record, because the identity came from the photo. Now a recognised rack has one identity that every photo of it shares, so the second photo updates the same records instead of making new ones.

    Records saved earlier under the old code are moved across by a visible re-label step the admin sees and approves. It never happens quietly, and it never renames or moves the customer's own rack.

  6. Decide per device, not per port

    Live since 18 September

    A brand new rack came up with 290 separate decisions, one for every port, which would have raised 290 tickets. Now a switch is one decision and its ports follow it, and a whole rack can be handed to one person in one move.

    Measured on the live system on 18 September: the same rack produced 191 items, of which 170 were ports folded under their switch, leaving 9 decisions for a person.

  7. The rules are enforced, not just shown

    Live since 18 September

    The server itself now refuses anything outside the rules. A technician can only compare and send. Approve and reject are refused until somebody has actually been asked. Every step is written to an audit trail. This was built in a second stream of work and joined with everything above, and it went out to the demo on 18 September.

    Checked on the live system, not only in tests: approving a device nobody has been asked about is refused with "assign first", a single port cannot be decided on its own, and a whole-rack decision mixed with a single item is refused outright.

  8. Approvals are being rebuilt as their own application

    In progress

    The approval screens are moving out of the phone app and the admin website into a small application of their own, and approval plans are moving from files into a proper database. It is a large change, under way in the second stream. The technician's compare and send stays in the phone app. Every gap the reviews found is being built into the new version rather than patched onto the old one.

07 · What is next

What comes next, in order

Close the gaps the reviews found, prove it on the phone, then build the missing line carefully.

  1. Fix the account that belongs to no organisation

    The platform owner account is shown checks it cannot open, including its own, because the list and the page use two different rules. The rule is agreed: a check belongs to the organisation that raised it; when the raiser has no organisation, only that account sees it; and the list uses the same test as the page, so a row you cannot open is never shown. Until it is fixed, the workflow is demonstrated as an organisation admin.

  2. Close the two gaps in re-opening a rack

    Re-opening a rack must keep its identity and must never slip back to the old code. Both were found by review and neither is fixed yet.

  3. Check it on the phone

    Ports folded under their switch, a whole rack handed over in one move, and a technician who can only compare and send. All three on the simulator before anybody else sees them.

  4. Two small fixes

    A faster first compare for a big new rack, and keeping earlier work when a rack is re-opened.

  5. Connect a rack the customer already has

    When the record already holds the rack and its devices, connect to them as a clear action the admin chooses, never silently, never renaming or moving the customer's rack, and matching its existing devices by shelf rather than creating new ones.

  6. Build the missing line: which box is which switch

    The reworked design in section 04, built behind the same approval path, writing confirmed matches only.

  7. Later

    Reading labels and barcodes, and the stronger checks that enterprise hardware makes possible, once such hardware is available to test on.

08 · How we keep it safe

How we keep it safe

The record belongs to the customer. A wrong write is worse than no write, so the work is checked before, during and after.

The rules that never bend

  • The person at the rack never decides. They report what they saw.
  • The admin hands a difference to somebody before deciding on it.
  • A ticket somebody answered is not an approval. It comes back to the admin.
  • Only approved changes are written, and nothing is written if the record changed in the meantime.
  • Nothing is ever deleted, and a guess is never written.

Designs are attacked before any code is written

Each new design goes to independent reviewers whose only job is to break it. Twice this week they did, and the design was reworked before a line of code existed.

The first no-duplicates design

It would have quietly merged the racks of two customers who happened to use the same rack name, and would have written a whole room of racks into one. Rejected, redesigned, then built.

The first which-box design

It would have turned one press of a button into "confirmed by a person", split one switch into two devices, and broken the photo to record line that works today. Rejected and reworked.

Joining two streams of work

The joined work passed every test, and reading it for meaning still found what no test had caught: a re-label that could never be decided, a screen whose only button the server always refused, a plan that counted as finished while tickets were still open, a retry that could never succeed after a partly failed save, and a new port that could be approved from a desk. The first two are fixed. The rest are being built into the rebuilt approvals.

Two screens, two rules, one wrong answer

Within hours of the rules going live, the second stream measured the running system and found the list of checks and the page for one check using different tests. An account outside every organisation was shown rows it could never open. No test caught it, because each rule was right on its own; only using the system as a real person did. It is written down, the rule is agreed, and the fix is being built.

Two people working on one codebase

Two streams are changing this system at the same time. Each builds in its own copy and only joins the main line when the main line is clean, so neither can quietly overwrite the other's unfinished work.

Every build is checked twice

An independent reviewer reads each finished build and runs the tests. A second reviewer then checks the fixes. The automatic tests run on every change, and they hold the promises above in place.

Every screen on this page is the running system between 11 and 18 September 2026: the phone app and the admin website at racktrack.ai, and the ServiceNow test instance whose tickets RackTrack raised and resolved. The rack is a real rack and the photo is the real photo taken of it. Work is tracked under SPRTMS-1636.
